current:
Alexander presents a pragmatic-prudential argument for accepting free will, using key Greek terms: πρακτέον (prakteon, one must act), ἀσφαλέστερον (asphalesteron, safer), κίνδυνος (kindynos, risk/danger).

Argument structure:
Premise 1: If determinism is true and we believe in free will, we lose nothing (our actions were fated anyway)
Premise 2: If free will is true and we believe in determinism, we risk moral disaster (abandoning responsibility)
Premise 3: It is rational to minimize risk of catastrophic outcomes
Conclusion: It is pragmatically safer (ἀσφαλέστερον) to believe in free will

This anticipates Pascal's Wager by ~1400 years, applied to metaphysics rather than theology. Alexander argues that even if we cannot resolve the theoretical question, practical reason dictates acceptance of free will. One of the earliest known "pragmatic" arguments in ancient philosophy - reasoning from practical consequences rather than theoretical proof.
proposed: In De Fato 36 Alexander turns the determinists' own act of arguing against them. He grants that if the determinists are compelled by surrounding causes (αἴτια περιεστῶτα) to assert their thesis, they deserve pardon (συγγινώσκειν αὐτοῖς ἄξιον) and there is no point disputing with them, since the cause of everything said and believed would be 'the power of the surrounding circumstances'. But if instead we have the power (ἐξουσίαν ἔχομεν) to say something better or worse, this already shows that something is up to us (ἐφ' ἡμῖν). The argument is thus a self-refutation charge against the determinist's act of reasoned assertion, not a prudential 'wager'.
